paras: The Oatmanville shooting of Augustin Agirer was an attack on August 8, 1882, near Oatmanville in Travis County, Texas, in which two young white men shot Agirer and another Mexican, Redel, on the road home from a justice court where Agirer had won a complaint against their friend. Early reports said Agirer was killed, but an Austin dispatch the next day said both men were still alive and expected to die, and the shooters escaped arrest with help from friends.

According to R. H. Brumby, the attorney for the state, William Boston, Lewis Wade, James LaRue and a fourth man passed Agirer's house on Richard Young's place about ten days earlier, and one of them shot at Agirer's dog. When Agirer asked why, Boston leveled his pistol and threatened to shoot him, and Agirer swore out a complaint in Justice Pace's court charging Boston with carrying a six-shooter and with assault. At the trial on August 8 Boston was fined twenty-five dollars, and Brumby said his companions were "very bitter in their denunciation of the Mexican" and threatened to take Boston from the officer. A posse brought Boston to Austin, while Wade and LaRue rode off at the same time in the opposite direction.

The Statesman's account came from Agirer's wife, as relayed by Mrs. Young: she, her husband and Redel were nearly home when Wade and LaRue overtook them and told Agirer he "either had to take a whipping or die." When Agirer began to beg, she said, LaRue shot him without another word, and she ran to the Young house for help. Returning with Mrs. Young, she found Agirer dead, by Mrs. Young's account, and Redel shot in the breast and apparently mortally wounded, with the attackers gone.
A Dallas Herald dispatch from Austin described the shooters as two boys aged 17 and 19 and said the Mexicans had testified against their friend in a concealed-weapons case.

A Black man first carried word of the shooting to Austin, and a man named Madden who came with him was arrested there for carrying a six-shooter. An inquest was announced for the morning of August 9 and a posse went after Wade and LaRue, but no inquest result appears in the coverage. On August 10 officers returned without the men, reporting that friends were supplying them with provisions and whisky and threatening to kill any officer who tried to arrest them, as well as the justice who had fined Boston. The same dispatch said citizens of Oatmanville were afraid to give officers any information, and no report of an arrest or trial was found.

Texas papers treated the shooting as an unprovoked crime: the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman headlined it "A Double Killing" with "The Murderers Still at Large," though it declined comment until the inquest. The Dallas Herald's Austin correspondent called it "wholly uncalled for, the men being peaceable, industrious farmers," and its first brief was reprinted in the Dallas Weekly Herald.

Outside Texas the story ran only as a one-sentence Austin wire in Maine papers, headed "A Sanguinary Conflict" in the Portland Daily Press and "Fight Between Americans and Mexicans" in the Daily Kennebec Journal. That wire garbled the names as "Lane and Wade" and "Algir and Reidell" and described a fight in which both Mexicans were shot dead, with none of the local detail about the trial or the ultimatum.

The reports disagree on the outcome: the Herald's first brief and the Statesman said Agirer was killed, the wire said both Mexicans died, and later Austin dispatches of August 9 and 10 said both were still alive though expected to die. The local accounts, based on the wife's statement and the prosecuting attorney, describe a one-sided shooting, while the wire's "fight" gives no source.

reader.title: Oatmanville shooting of Augustin Agirer
bases: Two armed white men overtook a Mexican complainant and his companions on the road after a trial, told him to 'take a whipping or die' and shot him and a second Mexican (A2, A1); the victims were Mexican, not Black (A1, A2, A4).

The Austin Statesman's local account (A2), the Herald's Austin specials (A1, A6) and the national Austin wire (A4) agree that two men shot two Mexicans near Oatmanville, though they differ on whether either died.

Maine papers ran the Austin wire as 'A Sanguinary Conflict' and 'Fight Between Americans and Mexicans', presenting it as a mutual fight.
